Copper Semis Service – Copper Wirerod Chapter 2 Developments in Trade 2 - 1 # Chapter 2 Trade ## 1. Overview & Methodology This chapter briefly reviews trends in international trade for the market segments of: - **Copper Wirerod** - **Single Strand Copper Wire** - **Stranded Copper Wire** The latter two represent the two final processing stages before the wire is insulated which then transformed into an insulated wire and cable product. They are often referred to the drawn wire products in this chapter. The sum of copper wirerod and drawn wire products then provides an account of copper that the wire and cable industry consumes. The trade developments for each of the three segments, copper wirerod, single strand copper wire and stranded copper wire are discussed individually in this chapter. Key areas that are highlighted include world trade volumes (‘000 tonnes) and world trade values (US$) as well as Data: CRU
2 - 2 Copper Semis – Copper Wirerod Chapter 2 Developments in Trade identifying the leading exporters and importers for each segment. Recent trade trends and corresponding factors affecting trade for the segment are also discussed. The data set analysed in this chapter is obtained from both reporting and derived country searches on the Global Trade Atlas resources, which includes the export and import data for each market segment from 2000 to 2007. This is the most recent data available and takes into account any official revisions to past data. For each segment, trade volume is reported in two ways. Firstly, it is reported directly by Country Z that imports or exports wirerod and drawn wire. A derived trade volume figure is also reported by all the countries that trade with Country Z. We then compare the two numbers and check if they are consistent with each other. Adjustments are made where there is a major discrepancy, which is likely to happen when countries misclassify or misreport their trade volumes. Misclassification is especially common for copper wirerod as a lot of countries report it under the copper rod, bar and section category (HS code 740710). For this reason, we also obtain the official copper rod, bar and profiles trade data and fit it into gaps of the copper wirerod trade where appropriate. The final database used for discussion and the tables presented in this chapter are therefore our closest estimates of the actual trade volume. Misreporting is common as well. On an annual basis between 55-60% of all reported trade in copper rods, bars and profiles is actually copper wirerod, which on average equates to around 200,000 tonnes per year. The trade data presented here is therefore, we believe, the best overall assessment of world trade in copper wirerod and drawn wire available to the industry. Appendix A towards the end of the volume provides additional tables not included in this chapter but

which are relevant to trade developments in these segments. 

In this particular section, an overview is given for **world trade in copper wirerod and drawn wire products** from different perspectives in order to detect any obvious trade trend in the industry. It will start by looking at **world trade volumes in tonnage** and **in value** , then **by type and by region** . 

In the following sections, it will examine **world trade in copper wirerod, single strand wire and stranded copper wire** .  Similar approach will be taken, with an overview given to trade in each product type, followed by factors affect that particular trade flow.

### **Main Findings of World Trade in Copper Wirerod and Drawn Wire Products** 

In 2007, world trade volume in copper wirerod and drawn wire products amounted to 3,351,000 tonnes compare to 2,612,000 tonnes in 2000, which indicates a compound average growth rate of 3.2%. In US dollars, world trade value in copper wirerod and drawn wire products was US$5.9B in 2007 compared to US$23.5B in 2000. 

- Among the total world trade volume in 2007, the majority (83%) was copper wirerod, 11% was single strand wire and 6% was stranded copper wire. In 2000, copper wirerod was 80% of world trade in copper wirerod and drawn wire products, of which 15% was single strand wire and 6% was stranded copper wire. The percentages of copper wirerod, single strand wire and stranded copper wire in world trade have not changed greatly since 2000 while the growth rate of trade volume has experienced more fluctuation. 

- World trade volume growth reached its peak in 2004 at 13%. The growth rate then fell to 5% in 2006 and to

3% in 2007. It appears that the growth rate changes occurred mostly in copper wirerod trade while growth rate in single strand wire and stranded copper wire were more stable. 2 - 4 Copper Semis – Copper Wirerod Chapter 2 Developments in Trade - Europe has been a net exporter of copper wirerod and drawn wire products consistently while Rest of the World (RoW) and Americas have been net importers. Asia had been a net importer until 2006 when it turned into a net exporter. Overall, the trade deficit in RoW and the trade surplus in Europe have increased gradually over the period 2000 to 2006, which indicates further specialisation in production. In 2007, the trade deficit in Americas was down 34% year-on-year to 77,000 tonnes; the trade surplus in Europe increased by 21% year-on-year to 410,000 tonnes; the trade surplus in Asia has gone from 25,000 tonnes in 2006 to 21,000 tonnes in 2007; and the trade deficit in RoW increased by 43% year-on-year to 354,000 tonnes. - In the Americas, the United States, Central America and South America (excluding Brazil and Chile) are the main net importers while Canada and Chile are the main net exporters of copper wirerod and drawn wire products. Interesting trade trends are detected from Brazil and Mexico. Brazil had been a net exporter of copper wirerod and drawn wire products from 2000 to 2006 but it became a net importer in 2007 with a trade deficit of 3,000 tonnes. Mexico was also a net exporter in 2000 to 2001 but it became a net importer from 2002 onwards. It has a significant trade deficit of 103,000 tonnes in 2007. - In Europe, France, Benelux, Germany, Russia, Poland and Turkey are the main net exporters of copper wirerod and drawn wire products. Among all European countries, Russia was the biggest net exporter and it has a trade surplus of 513,000 tonnes in 2007, including substantial tonnage delivered from stocks accumulated by mills or traders to Middle Eastern and North African consumers, but misreported in official trade statistics. On the other hand, Italy and United Kingdom have been the main net importers. In 2007, United Kingdom’s trade deficit has increased by almost nine times from 2006 to 144,000 tonnes following the ending of UK production in 2006. Interestingly, Nordic Countries had been a net exporter from 2000 to 2004 but in 2005 they turned into a net importer of 10,000 tonnes. The trade deficit has decreased since then. 2 - 14 Copper Semis – Copper Wirerod Chapter 2 Developments in Trade In the following we have classified issues that could affect trade flows of copper wirerod and drawn wire products into seven major factors, including exchange rates, transportation, consumption, production, cost savings, national standards and company ownership. - Movements in exchange rates can influence trade as a rise in a currency’s value means its exports become less attractive to other countries and vice versa. For example, at the moment the US dollar is fairly weak, which makes exports from the US cheaper. On the other hand, imports going into the US will become more expensive so the import volume is likely to go down. - A country’s transportation links and location are crucial since they affect accessibility to the country’s trade partners and therefore its market share within the tradable region. For instance, if a wirerod consumer is located in northeast part of US it might be more economic to import from Canada then purchasing domestically from say Arizona. - Consumption and production have a direct impact on trade as the imbalance between the two is the fundamental driver for trade flows. This also relates to cost savings as some countries are more efficient producing wirerod mainly because it has lower labour or fixed costs and as a result they export more wirerod. - Ownership of a company could also affect trade flows. For example, a wirerod consumer located in Taiwan that is 100% owned by another company in China then it might internally source its input from the mother company in China because it is their company policy. - Other factors include national standards, common languages and history. Country Z would be more likely to trade with Country X then Country Y if Country Z and X share the same languages and national standards. In the following sections, we will examine the factors that affect trade flows by type. The first one we will look at is copper wirerod. Copper Semis Service – Copper Wirerod Chapter 2 Developments in Trade 2 - 15 ## 2.2 Copper Wirerod Copper wirerod is a heavy and low value added product. The

refore trade of copper wirerod can only occur within a certain distance from the mill.  As a result, one would expect trade flows changes are mainly caused by demand or other issues from the neighbouring area. The total world trade volume of copper wirerod in 2007 was 2.8Mt, which is a 4.7% increase year-onyear, versus 2.1Mt in 2000. 

Regions that have gained share from copper wirerod world import volume during 2000 to 2007 are South and Central America, Eastern and Central Europe and RoW. Eastern and Central European imports have gone from 6% in 2000 to 12% in 2007 while RoW has increased from 7% in 2000 to 17% in 2007. The share of South and Central America has increased from 4% in 2000 to 5% in 2007. North America and Western Europe saw a decrease in their share of total import volume during 2000 to 2007. Western Europe had the largest share in 2007 that accounted for 36% of world import volume while Northeast Asia was the smallest importer in 2007 with a 1% share. Developing Asia’s share has gone from 20% to 15%. 

Regions that have gained share from copper wirerod world export volume during 2000 to 2007 are Eastern and Central Europe, Developing Asia and RoW. Eastern and Central European exports have gone from 6% in 2000 to 23% in 2007 while Developing Asia has also increased from 3% in 2000 to 9% in 2007. North America, Western Europe and Northeast Asia all saw a decrease in their share in total import volume during 2000 to 2007.  The biggest drop indicated was in Northeast Asia, from 18% in 2000 to 8% in 2007. Western Europe is the largest importer in 2007 with a 38% share of world import volume while RoW and South and Central America are the smallest importers in 2007 with a 5% share. 

Developing Asia has been a major net importer since 2000. However, its copper wirerod trade deficit has fallen significantly by 60% over the last 5 years since peaking in 2002 because of decreased import volume and increased export volume. The region has a trade deficit of 167,000 tonnes, an 8% increase year-on-year in 2007, which could possibly be a result of a restocking cycle. Eastern and Central Europe has become a major net exporter with a trade surplus of 330,000 tonnes in 2007, which is an increase of 79% year-on-year. South and Central America had been a net exporter until 2007 when it became a net importer with a trade deficit of 3,000 tonnes of copper wirerod. With trade deficit of RoW growing larger, it is expected that Western Europe and Northeast Asia will export less in the following years. 

When looking at trade by country, France is the largest exporter and the United States the largest importer back in 2000. France exported 273,000 tonnes of copper wirerod, which represented more than 13% of world export volume. The United States imported 297,000 tonnes of copper wirerod in 2007, which is 14% of world import volume.  In 2007, Russia has become the leading exporter and exported 516,000 tonnes of copper wirerod, including a significant vol

ume from accumulated stocks (either at mills or traders) and which was misclassified in trade statistics but imported by the Middle East and North Africa. #### **Factors Affect Copper Wirerod Trade** As a large proportion of copper wirerod is used in the building sector, one of the most significant factors that affect trade in copper wirerod is therefore the demand from building activities. Infrastructure boom opportunities from emerging nations are particularly influential to trade as most of the time these countries would not be able to supply its demand domestically and would import wirerod from overseas. It is reasonable to expect a positive relationship between a country’s planned infrastructure expenditure and wirerod imports. According to Merrill Lynch’s research report in June, China is going to spend more than US$700 billion on its infrastructure, more than any other country, over the next three years. No surprise that China was the second biggest importer of copper wirerod in 2007. Benefiting from high oil prices, the Gulf region is second and is estimated at US$400 million. From our data, the Middle East is one of the world’s fastest growing economies and its wirerod import volum

e has increased from 76,000 tonnes to 290,000 tonnes of copper wirerod. India is estimated at US$240 billion while its import volume has risen three-folded since 2002. Brazil imported 33,000 tonnes of wirerod to feed its US$225 billion infrastructure expenditure. Turkey is expected to spend US$60 billion in the next three years. Its wirerod imports have increased drastically from 10,000 tonnes in 2002 to 55,000 tonnes in 2007. Our data also shows that South African import volume has more than doubled to 18,000 tonnes since 2002 and the country is going to spend US$60 billion on infrastructure. Copper Semis Service – Copper Wirerod Chapter 2 Developments in Trade 2 - 21 Another important factor affecting trade is the US slowdown. It is known that a housing bubble burst in late 2006 and since then the US economy has been going downhill, with the construction sector being the hardest hit. As the residential construction sector outlook continues to weaken after the credit crunch, latest data suggests that housing starts and building permits have decreased by more than 20% year-on-year in June. A significant 3.1 million tonnes, equivalent to of wirerod production is fed into the building sector so a drop in demand means a negative impact on wirerod imports. Evidently, exports from neighbour countries into the United States have fallen drastically by 30% year-on-year in 2007. Exchange rate movements could have an effect on trade flows as well. From OECD’s data, the US Dollar per SDR (Special Drawing Rights) has depreciated by 17.5% in the last eight years. SDR is defined using a basket of major currencies used in international trade and finance. Therefore, as SDR can by more US Dollars, US$1 carries less value and it would be less attractive to import into the United States. On the other hand, when US Dollar per SDR is appreciating, it encourages other countries to import into the United States. Looking at the graph here, it indicates that wirerod import volume could be sensitive to exchange rates as it dropped whenever the US Dollar depreciated especially in 2003 and 2007. 2 - 22 Copper Semis – Copper Wirerod Chapter 2 Developments in Trade

The North American trade deficit has gone down by 70% year-on-year to 3,000 tonnes whereas that of Developing Asia has decreased from 105,000 tonnes in 2006 to 82,000 tonnes in 2007. However, compared to wirerod, trade can occur slightly further from the wire mill. Total world import volume of single strand wire totalled 371,000 tonnes in 2007, which is a 7% drop from 2006. Comparing data in 2000 and 2007, Western Europe has increased its share of world trade volume from a 33% share to a 40% share while the Eastern and Central European share has increased to a 7% share. The North American share of import shrunk from 13% to 7% while South and Central America went from 1% to 2%. Developing Asia has also lost some share to the RoW as its share gone down from a 43% share to a 35% share while that of RoW has doubled in 2007. As for the exports market, the ranking has not changed much from 2000 as Western Europe is still the major exporter. However, Developing Asia has gained a significant share going from 8% to 15% in 2007. Eastern and Central Europe also saw a four-folded increase in its global export market share. Leading

exporters of single strand wire in 2000 were Taiwan at 75,000 tonnes, Germany next at 53,000 tonnes and France at 33,000 tonnes. In 2007, Germany was ranked first at 67,000 tonnes, Taiwan next at 56,000 tonnes and Turkey at 30,000 tonnes. For imports, China was the largest importer in 2000 importing 127,000 tonnes of single strand wire. France imported 27,000 tonnes and United States at 22,000 tonnes. China is still importing the most at 95,000 tonnes in 2007, Benelux next at 25,000 tonnes and Germany at 23,000 tonnes. In the chart of world net trade in single strand wire, it is shown that Developing Asia’s trade deficit has deteriorated since 2004. It also fell by 22% year-on-year in 2007. Northeast Asia has correspondingly seen a decrease in its trade surplus since 2005. The Western European trade surplus in single strand wire has decreased by 32% while the trade deficit of Eastern and Central Europe has decreased by 10%. Both North America and South and Central America saw trade deficit going down by half. This could be a result of dampened demand from the US automotive market as well as the depreciation of the US Dollar. #### **Factors that Affect Single Strand Wire Trade** There are four big factors that are likely to influence recent trade flows. First of all, a country is most likely to benefit from low cost production. As producers seek to enhance their profitability, they take an advantage from sourcing low production costs countries, which is also known as globalisation. From the above, we have seen exports growing rapidly from Eastern and Central Europe. This is partly due to lower labour and fixed costs in Eastern and Central Europe compared to some countries like the UK. A better example to illustrate how a country’s trade benefit from low cost production would be Indonesia, where exports of single strand wire have increased by 28% throughout the last 8 years. Indonesia not only has low production costs, it is also located in an accessible region where it could export economically to Northeast Asia, Developing Asia as well as Australia. 2 - 32 Copper Semis – Copper Wirerod Chapter 2 Developments in Trade ##### Table 2.11: World exports of single strand wire 2000-2007 by major country & region ('000 tonnes) ||**2000**|**2001**|**2002**|**2003**|**2004**|**2005**|**2006**|**2007**|**_2001_**|**_2002_**|**_2003_**

2 - 40 Copper Semis – Copper Wirerod Chapter 2 Developments in Trade ## 2.5 **Stranded Copper Wire** Looking at the global net trade flows of stranded copper wire, South and Central America has been increasing its trade deficit. Developing Asia’s trade deficit peaked at 10,000 tonnes in 2006 but fell by 2,000 tonnes in 2007. The Eastern and Central European trade surplus has been decreasing over the years while Western Europe has turned into a net exporter since 2004. Total import volume of stranded copper wire totalled 146,000 tonnes in 2000 and 187,000 tonnes in 2007, respectively. Western Europe has lost a significant 10% share, while Eastern and Central Europe has picked up a 10% share of the import market over the past eight years as wire and cable production has migrated from Western Europe to Eastern and Central Europe. Developing Asia and South and Central America has also gained share in the same period with the former region now holds 9% share and the latter holds 5%. This is due to the expansion in automotive wiring harness assembly in the region. In terms of exports, the proportions have almost stayed the same as 2000. In 2007, North America has decreased its share from 25% to 22%. Western Europe’s share has increased from 47% to 48%, whereas Eastern and Central Europe’s share has increased by 4% points. Northeast Asia’s share has shrunk while Developing Asia’s has gone up from 3% to 4%. Leading importers of stranded copper wire in 2000 are Mexico at 19,000 tonnes, France at 13,000 tonnes and United States at 11,000 tonnes. In 2007, the import market is more evenly distributed with Mexico still the biggest importer at 17,000 tonnes, Hungary and Italy both at 13,000 tonnes, Canada and France in third place at 12,000 tonnes. The leading exporter of stranded copper wire in 2000 was United States with 34,000 tonnes exported. Germany was in second place in 2000 and went up to first at 45,000 tonnes in 2007. United States is at 39,000 tonnes in 2007, slightly behind Germany. Turkey stays the same at third place with exports increased by 10,000 tonnes to 31,000 tonnes. #### **Factors that Affect Stranded Copper Wire Trade** Exchange rate remains an important factor that affects stranded copper wire trade flows. Eastern and Central European exports had been growing since 2000 at a fast rate and reached peak in 2005 at 47,000 tonnes. Turkish

exports then dropped by 18% year-on-year in 2006 while Polish exports fell by 25% year-on-year in 2007. It is suspected that Turkish exports to the US were particularly discouraged by the depreciation of the US Dollar. According to data provided by OECD, New Turkish Lira per US Dollar increased by 6% year-on-year while exports to the US decreased by 18% year-on-year in 2006. On the other hand, exports from the US have been growing since 2003. Reduction in exports from Poland mainly comes from Romania, Czech Republic and Bulgaria where domestic production is at a fast-growing rate. Imports are rising in some major countries in Western Europe. German imports went up by 13% year-on-year in 2007, Italy is by 8% and Benelux by 75%. The whole Western European region recorded an increase of 5.3% year-on-year in 2007. Compare to 2002, the whole region is importing 10,000 tonnes more in 2007, equivalent to a 32% increase.
